summary: Something measured repeatedly, drawn against time — the workhorse chart: MOS per trunk, latency per site, calls per minute.

figma.note: Drawn on the Charts page as `Chart / Time series`. The frame, the furniture and the colours are there; the scale, the gap handling and the crosshair are behaviour and are not — see the page's notes frame.

pairs.dont: Assign colours by position in the filtered list, so hiding one trunk repaints every trunk below it.
pairs.do: Give each series a stable `id` and pass the whole list; the chart keeps each series on the slot it was built with.
pairs.why: People read a colour as a name. If filtering out Sydney turns Melbourne from purple to blue, every reading taken before the filter is now wrong, and nothing on screen says so.

pairs.dont: Fill a missing reading with 0, so a trunk that stopped reporting draws a cliff to the floor.
pairs.do: Pass `null`. The line breaks, and the table says "No data".
pairs.why: An endpoint going quiet and an endpoint scoring zero are different incidents with different responses. A line to the floor reports the second when the first happened.

pairs.dont: Fill under several series at once and hope the overlaps read.
pairs.do: Fill one series; draw several as lines.
pairs.why: Overlapping translucent fills are the chart that looks informative and answers nothing — no overlap can be read as a value, and the series drawn last looks the largest. The component refuses `area` past one series rather than drawing it badly.

pairs.dont: Put latency and call count on one chart with a scale down each side.
pairs.do: Two charts, or one chart with both measures indexed to a common base.
pairs.why: A dual axis lets whoever drew it decide where the lines cross, because the two scales are chosen independently. It is the single most common way a chart misleads, and there is no API for it here.

pairs.dont: Generate a seventh colour when there are more series than slots.
pairs.do: Fold the tail into one "Other" series, or facet into small multiples.
pairs.why: The palette has six slots, and it has six because three of the declared eight could not be told apart from the others — corporate blue sits 7° from brand blue, IR lime is outside the usable lightness band, and teal cannot clear blue in both modes. A generated hue lands wherever there is room, which is usually next to a colour already in use. Both alternatives are decisions about the data, so the chart warns rather than deciding silently.

pairs.dont: Rely on the hover crosshair as the only way to read a number.
pairs.do: Render the data table visibly where exact values matter, and keep the chart for the shape.
pairs.why: The crosshair is pointer-only. Someone navigating by keyboard, or reading the page without a pointer, gets the visually-hidden table — which is the right answer for a screen reader and no answer at all for a sighted keyboard user.

a11y: The plot is `aria-hidden` and the numbers are carried by a visually-hidden table, so a screen reader gets the data rather than a shape it cannot see.
`label` is required and becomes the table's caption — it is what the chart is of, in a sentence.
A gap reads as "No data" in the table rather than as an empty cell, which would be indistinguishable from a cell that failed to render.

The legend is always present from two series up and never for one, where the title names the series. Swatches carry identity; the text stays in ink, because a light series colour is illegible as text.
Legend toggles are real buttons with `aria-pressed`, and the last visible series cannot be hidden.
⚠️ The crosshair is pointer-only. There is no keyboard equivalent yet — see the Do and Don't.

Amber (slot 5) and IR red (slot 2) separate by only ΔE ~7 for protanopia and deuteranopia — inside the floor band, which is legal only with a second channel. The legend, the tooltip's series names and the data table are that channel; a chart stripped of all three should direct-label its lines.
